Simulate the Literature a Plan Came From and Audit How Often It Works

Source: R/bucss-sensitivity.R
ss_buc_sensitivity.Rd

ss_buc_sensitivity takes a plan returned by any ss_buc_* function and asks the question the method's assurance claim is really about: if the true effect were a particular value, and a literature published only the prior studies that reached significance, how often would a plan built this way actually reach the target power?

Usage

ss_buc_sensitivity(object, true_ncp, replications = 1000L, seed = NULL)

Arguments

object

A plan returned by any ss_buc_* function.

true_ncp

The assumed true noncentrality parameter of the prior study's design, on the same scale as the ncp_adjusted row of object. Required; there is deliberately no default.

replications

Number of published prior studies to simulate. At an assurance of .80 the default of 1000 gives attainment_with_refusals a Monte Carlo standard error near .013, and 10000 about .004; both are reported. The standard error of attainment, which counts only the issued plans, is larger when many prior studies are refused.

seed

Optional random number seed. NULL (the default) draws from the caller's own random number stream, advancing it as any simulation does. When a seed is supplied, the caller's random number state and generator are restored on exit (and no state is left behind if the caller had none). A seed reproduces a result only under the same random number generators (see RNGkind).

Value

An object of class bucss_sensitivity, a data.frame with columns term and value carrying the assumed true parameter and the plan's own ncp_adjusted for comparison, the number of replications, the publication and refusal rates, the two attainment rates each with its Monte Carlo standard error, the sample size the true effect requires, and the quartiles of the sample sizes the simulated plans called for. The design, the effect tested (for designs with one), the sample size unit, the requested assurance, and the requested desired_power travel as attributes. If every simulated prior study is refused, attainment, its standard error, and the quartiles are NA, with a warning.

Details

The bias and uncertainty correction rests on a claim about the long run. At assurance = .80, eight replications in ten should reach the target power, the probability that a study's test rejects the null hypothesis when the effect is present (Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027). That claim is a statement about a whole literature, and a user planning one study never sees it exercised.

This function exercises it on the user's own numbers. It reads the design and the planning inputs off the plan you pass it, simulates prior studies of that design from a true effect you name, discards the ones a literature would not have published (those failing to reach significance at alpha_prior), runs the same planner on each survivor, and reports what happened.

You must name the true effect. There is no default, deliberately. Defaulting to the corrected estimate would be convenient and circular: it would ask the method to grade its own answer. true_ncp is on the same scale as the ncp_adjusted the plan reports, so the plan's own value is the natural anchor. Run the function at that value, at a fraction of it, and at a multiple of it; the interesting reading is how fast the attainment rate falls when the truth is smaller than the corrected estimate.

Reading the output. A plan attains the target when its sample size is at least the sample size the true effect actually requires, which is reported as size_at_true_effect. Two attainment rates are given, and the difference between them is not a rounding detail:

  • attainment counts only the prior studies for which the method issued a plan. This is what a user experiences.

  • attainment_with_refusals counts a refusal (the planner's stop when the corrected noncentrality parameter is zero, or, for a design the planner reduces to a balanced one, its stop when a published statistic is not significant at the balanced design's degrees of freedom) as attaining, because declining to plan is the limiting case of an arbitrarily conservative plan. This is the quantity the assurance guarantee is about, and it should land on assurance. For a prior study that the planner reduces to a balanced design it can land above, because the planner is then conservative: about .84 at an assurance of .80 for prior groups of 10 and 90 in the independent t test.

When the refusal rate is high the first number sits well below assurance, and that is not a defect: it is the visible price of the method refusing rather than guessing. Its expected value is (assurance - refusal_rate)/(1 - refusal_rate), or more when attainment_with_refusals lands above assurance.

What this can and cannot detect. The prior studies are drawn from the sampling distribution the method assumes for that design, so this is a check that the correction and the planned sample size are internally right, and a demonstration of what publication bias does. It cannot detect a violated distributional assumption, since the simulation shares that assumption. For ss_buc_welch_t, in particular, it holds the variance ratio fixed at the value you supplied. For the regression planners the simulated prior studies follow the plan's own random_predictors setting, so audit a plan in the frame your research actually uses. For a within-subjects or split-plot plan made with epsilon below 1, the prior studies are drawn under the same approximation to a departure from sphericity that the planner corrects under, so the audit checks the method's internal consistency, not the approximation itself; the planner's help page reports how well the approximation holds against simulated raw data.

The package-wide verification ships with the package. This function audits one plan; the harness that verifies the planners themselves, including checks against raw simulated data that do not share the method's distributional assumptions (bivariate normal samples for the correlation planner, multivariate normal samples for a regression coefficient with random_predictors = TRUE, two-group normal samples for the Welch planner), is installed with BUCSS and can be rerun in a few seconds with source(system.file("tools", "verify_by_simulation.R", package = "BUCSS")).

References

Anderson, S. F., & Kelley, K. (2024). Sample size planning for replication studies: The devil is in the design. Psychological Methods, 29, 844–867. doi:10.1037/met0000520

Anderson, S. F., Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2017). Sample-size planning for more accurate statistical power: A method adjusting sample effect sizes for publication bias and uncertainty. Psychological Science, 28, 1547–1562. doi:10.1177/0956797617723724

Anderson, S. F., & Maxwell, S. E. (2017). Addressing the "replication crisis": Using original studies to design replication studies with appropriate statistical power. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 52, 305–324. doi:10.1080/00273171.2017.1289361

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8, 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

Taylor, D. J., & Muller, K. E. (1996). Bias in linear model power and sample size calculation due to estimating noncentrality. Communications in Statistics: Theory and Methods, 25, 1595–1610. doi:10.1080/03610929608831787

See also

ss_buc_independent_t and the other ss_buc_* planners, whose results this function takes as input.

Author

Ken Kelley (kkelley@nd.edu) and Samantha F. Anderson (samantha.f.anderson@asu.edu)

Examples

plan <- ss_buc_independent_t(t_observed = 3, n = c(50, 55), assurance = .80)
ncp <- plan$value[plan$term == "ncp_adjusted"]
ncp
#> [1] 1.338019

# Take the corrected estimate at face value as the truth. (200 replications
# keep the example quick: the rate counting refusals is good to about .03,
# the rate over issued plans to about .06. A reported audit deserves 10000.)
ss_buc_sensitivity(plan, true_ncp = ncp, replications = 200, seed = 113)
#>  term                          value 
#>  true_ncp                      1.34  
#>  ncp_adjusted                  1.34  
#>  replications                  200   
#>  publication_rate              0.263 
#>  refusal_rate                  0.57  
#>  attainment                    0.419 
#>  attainment_mcse               0.0532
#>  attainment_with_refusals      0.75  
#>  attainment_with_refusals_mcse 0.0306
#>  size_at_true_effect           233   
#>  size_q25                      98.8  
#>  size_median                   182   
#>  size_q75                      1050  
#> 
#> Design: Independent t test
#> Sample size unit: per group
#> Requested assurance: .80
#> Target power: .80

# And ask what happens if the truth is smaller than the correction assumed.
ss_buc_sensitivity(plan, true_ncp = .6 * ncp, replications = 200, seed = 113)
#>  term                          value 
#>  true_ncp                      0.803 
#>  ncp_adjusted                  1.34  
#>  replications                  200   
#>  publication_rate              0.125 
#>  refusal_rate                  0.735 
#>  attainment                    0.34  
#>  attainment_mcse               0.0651
#>  attainment_with_refusals      0.825 
#>  attainment_with_refusals_mcse 0.0269
#>  size_at_true_effect           642   
#>  size_q25                      137   
#>  size_median                   288   
#>  size_q75                      1034  
#> 
#> Design: Independent t test
#> Sample size unit: per group
#> Requested assurance: .80
#> Target power: .80
